scenes.tts: The first film separated living interactions from nonliving conditions. Can one nonliving condition predict where oysters might survive? Return to the same Virginia landscape. Follow salt from the upper James River to the mouth of the Bay.
scenes.visual: Open on the exact carried cross-section from the first film: mountain forest, James River, Chesapeake Bay, ocean. The two first-film lenses briefly overlap, then the GOLD nonliving lens enlarges over the water. A RED oyster question mark rides above a small boat. Reuse the COLOR MAP exactly: living things GREEN, nonliving conditions GOLD, fresh water BLUE, mixed estuary water TEAL, salt water PURPLE, oysters RED, labels TEXT white. Water and boat move continuously.
scenes.narration: The first film separated living interactions from nonliving conditions. Can one nonliving condition predict where oysters might survive? Return to the same Virginia landscape. Follow salt from the upper James River to the mouth of the Bay.

scenes.visual: Keep the river moving behind a short title card, 'Following Salt Down the James'. After two seconds, transform the title underline into the river path and return the boat to the upper tidal James.

scenes.tts: Salinity is the amount of salt dissolved in water. The upper James is fresh, while ocean water is salty. In the Chesapeake estuary, river water and ocean water mix. Salinity usually rises toward the Bay mouth, but the mixing zone can move.
scenes.visual: Fill most of the frame with the James-to-ocean water channel. BLUE water streams rightward while PURPLE ocean pulses leftward; their overlap transforms into TEAL. GOLD salt dots become denser toward the ocean. A large vertical gauge labeled 'salinity' rises as a marker travels downstream.
scenes.narration: Salinity is the amount of salt dissolved in water. The upper James is fresh, while ocean water is salty. In the Chesapeake estuary, river water and ocean water mix. Salinity usually rises toward the Bay mouth, but the mixing zone can move.

scenes.tts: A sampling boat starts at the upper tidal James. At each station, a probe measures the water below the surface. Each stop adds a point to the same river path. Watch the points climb as the boat moves toward the Bay.
scenes.visual: Boat travels left to right and pauses at the eight lesson stations. Lower a probe to an on-screen depth label '1 m'. At every stop, place a GOLD point above the river. Build a computed polyline from the lesson's exact means: 0.09, 1.32, 4.53, 11.54, 15.39, 20.67, 23.06, 25.78 PSU. Show station codes and values on screen only; do not speak them.
scenes.narration: A sampling boat starts at the upper tidal James. At each station, a probe measures the water below the surface. Each stop adds a point to the same river path. Watch the points climb as the boat moves toward the Bay.

scenes.tts: Now place an oyster beside the boat. Where along this fresh-to-salty path should oysters first find suitable water? Make a prediction before the boat moves again.
scenes.visual: Place one RED oyster icon beside the stationary boat near the middle of the route. Keep the computed salinity points visible. Add the large question 'Where does an oyster first fit?' A faint RED outline slides slowly along the route but does not settle.
scenes.narration: Now place an oyster beside the boat. Where along this fresh-to-salty path should oysters first find suitable water? Make a prediction before the boat moves again.

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction question for four and a half seconds. Water continues flowing and the faint oyster outline drifts slowly between stations. Do not reveal the suitable zone.

scenes.tts: The oyster first fits the brackish lower river, not the fresh upper river. Eastern oysters can die when water stays very low in salt for a long time. Wild oyster reefs grow in the lower James, where the water is mixed.
scenes.visual: Reveal a RED bracket over the brackish lower James and settle the oyster there. Show the guide range '10–28' on screen only beside the bracket and a warning 'below 5 for a long time' upstream. Grow a small reef in TEAL water; keep the fresh-water oyster ghosted out.
scenes.narration: The oyster first fits the brackish lower river, not the fresh upper river. Eastern oysters can die when water stays very low in salt for a long time. Wild oyster reefs grow in the lower James, where the water is mixed.

scenes.tts: The measured station means make the gradient visible. Low values sit upstream, and higher values sit near the Bay mouth. The difference between two stations must be calculated, not guessed from spacing. The lesson table lets you subtract exact values and test the oyster range.
scenes.visual: Lift the eight station points into a large frame-filling data strip while keeping the river directly beneath them. Highlight TF5.5 and LE5.4, then animate a subtraction slot between their on-screen values without revealing the result. Shade the on-screen oyster guide range behind qualifying points. All plotted heights come from the displayed means.
scenes.narration: The measured station means make the gradient visible. Low values sit upstream, and higher values sit near the Bay mouth. The difference between two stations must be calculated, not guessed from spacing. The lesson table lets you subtract exact values and test the oyster range.

scenes.tts: Range matches are not sharp borders. Widgeon grass can fit every station listed. The oyster's range overlaps the eelgrass stations near the Bay mouth. The crews measured water; they did not count organisms at those stations. Suitable salinity suggests habitat; it does not prove an organism was there.
scenes.visual: Transform the oyster-range shading into overlapping translucent GREEN range ribbons for widgeon grass and RED ribbons for oysters. Keep every station point visible. Change a check mark labeled 'salinity fits' into an open box labeled 'organism counted?' so the two claims cannot be confused.
scenes.narration: Range matches are not sharp borders. Widgeon grass can fit every station listed. The oyster's range overlaps the eelgrass stations near the Bay mouth. The crews measured water; they did not count organisms at those stations. Suitable salinity suggests habitat; it does not prove an organism was there.

scenes.tts: Salinity also shifts with rain and season. The boundary slides as fresh and salt water keep mixing. A station's value can change even though the river and Bay remain in place. One summer sample is a snapshot, not a permanent border.
scenes.visual: Return the ribbons to the river cross-section. Animate rain over the watershed while the BLUE-to-TEAL boundary slides toward the ocean; then ease the rain and let it move back. Station markers stay fixed while their gauge levels change. Label the whole motion 'schematic seasonal shift'.
scenes.narration: Salinity also shifts with rain and season. The boundary slides as fresh and salt water keep mixing. A station's value can change even though the river and Bay remain in place. One summer sample is a snapshot, not a permanent border.

scenes.tts: Salinity is powerful evidence, but it is only one condition. Light, temperature, water movement, predators, and food can matter too. Living interactions and nonliving conditions help decide what can live where. The strongest explanation connects the pattern to both sides of the ecosystem. Use the station data to test that rule, with limits.
scenes.visual: Keep the RED oyster in the lower James. GOLD arrows labeled 'salt', 'light', 'temperature', and 'water movement' join GREEN arrows labeled 'predators' and 'food'. Let the arrows balance around the oyster rather than one arrow controlling it. Then clear every label and leave the flowing James for the end card.
scenes.narration: Salinity is powerful evidence, but it is only one condition. Light, temperature, water movement, predators, and food can matter too. Living interactions and nonliving conditions help decide what can live where. The strongest explanation connects the pattern to both sides of the ecosystem. Use the station data to test that rule, with limits.
